entry.title: GST needs a consumption-based overhaul, not piecemeal refund reforms
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / GST needs a consumption-based overhaul, not piecemeal refund reformsGST needs a consumption-based overhaul, not piecemeal refund reforms

GST reforms must ensure immediate input-tax credits and refunds for businesses to reduce production costs, encourage investment and prevent tax cascading, argue Arbind Modi and Ajay Shah.

premium

A decade after GST was introduced, reforming input-tax credit and refund rules remains key to reducing the tax burden on production and investment, improving manufacturing competitiveness and supporting economic growth, argue Arbind Modi and Ajay Shah. | Illustration: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

Ajay ShahArbind Modi6 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 7:30 PM ISTIn a recent paper (Arbind Modi & Ajay Shah 2026, https://bit.ly/ModiShah2026), we identified a conceptual failure in India’s goods and services tax (GST). Restrictions on input-tax credit (ITC) and cash refunds compromise its character as a consumption-based value-added tax (VAT). These restrictions take Indian GST closer to the old-style turnover-based tax, burdening production and investment rather than taxing final consumption alone. The GST Council’s decisions of October represent small parametric reforms in the correct direction. What is required is the economic logic of GST. In India, this is one of the most important feasible reforms that would boost manufacturing, investment, exports and economic growth.  Economic efficiency requires that taxes fall on final household consumption, never on intermediate inputs or capital formation. GST is an accrual-based flow tax requiring symmetric treatment of positive and negative net liabilities. Each tax period, liability equals tax on outward supplies less ITC on legitimate business inputs, including goods, services and capital goods. When output tax exceeds ITC, the difference is payable to the government; when ITC exceeds output tax, the excess is paid by the government.  This is the gold standard of a consumption-type VAT. ITC or its refund is not a privilege granted to certain groups: it is the essence through which we graduate from the old Indian excise tax to GST with all the consequential economic gains. Capital-goods ITC must also be immediately available: delayed recovery imposes financing costs on investment and undermines neutrality. A credit not promptly recovered is worth less than its nominal amount, and it is tantamount to not getting ITC correctly.  At its October 8 meeting, the GST Council recommended extending inverted-duty refunds under Section 54(3) to input services from November 1, 2026, and including capital-goods ITC in refunds for zero-rated and qualifying inverted-duty supplies from April 1, 2027, subject to apportionment over 60 months. The apportionment applies to refunds, not to credits usable immediately against output tax. It also proposed removing selected restrictions under Section 17(5) and accelerating refunds through automated, risk-based processing. These decisions are in the correct direction and represent a part of the deficiencies identified in our paper.  Yet five-year apportionment introduces an income-type feature into a consumption-type VAT. Established businesses with sufficient output-tax liability (typically brownfield projects) can utilise capital-goods credits immediately, while newly established businesses with little initial output-tax liability (typically greenfield projects) depend on deferred cash refunds. The rule, therefore, discriminates against new enterprises undertaking identical investments. Like depreciation-based relief under an income-type VAT, deferred recovery reduces capital-goods credit in present-value terms, effectively taxing investment.  The GST Council has incrementally tried to address the refundability of ITC without changing the refund architecture. Cash refunds remain exceptions available in specified circumstances rather than the automatic consequence of negative net tax liability. Consider two businesses producing supplies taxed at 5 per cent and accumulating identical legitimate ITC. One qualifies for a refund because its material inputs attract a higher GST rate; the other does not because its excess credit arises mainly from services taxed at 18 per cent before outward supplies begin. The distinction is fully arbitrary when seen through the lens of economics. Under a consumption VAT, refund entitlement depends on excess legitimate credit, not the composition of inputs — goods, services or capital expenditure.  The 60-month rule also treats firms able to utilise credits immediately differently from those dependent on refunds, raising the latter’s effective investment costs. Selective relaxation of blocked-credit provisions is welcome but incomplete: restrictions on legitimate business expenditure, including factory civil works, still interrupt the credit chain and burden firms making substantial initial investments when output-tax liabilities are modest.  The October announcements represent parametric improvement within a conceptually confused framework. Refunds remain conditional while 60-month apportionment retains an income-type feature for businesses dependent on refunds. Unrecovered ITC raises production costs, discourages investment, and disadvantages domestic value addition relative to imported finished products, which cross the border free of domestic input-tax cascading. Faster processing cannot compensate for denying refunds of legitimate credits. The measure of reform is not the number of additional categories made refundable but whether tax on business inputs and investment is eliminated in economic terms.  We now have a decade of experience with GST and there is a lot of understanding of how it works. The reform priority now is to replace exception-based refunds with a comprehensive, symmetric mechanism. All legitimate business-input taxes should qualify for immediate credit, with positive net liabilities paid to the government and negative liabilities promptly refunded, subject to anti-abuse safeguards.  This requires the GST architecture proposed by us in the Thirteenth Finance Commission Task Force architecture: a broader consumption base, fewer exemptions, and a low uniform rate around 12 per cent to reduce classification disputes and manipulation. Much of the immediate fiscal burden from refunds would be transitional rather than permanent. Previously blocked credits, however, carry a separate recurring fiscal cost. Eliminating taxes on production and investment would improve resource allocation, stimulate investment, and expand the tax base. Transitional costs must be managed, and not used to justify permanent economic distortions.  A comprehensive GST with a single 12 per cent rate, including gold consumption but excluding investment bullion, could generate sufficient revenue to finance the transition and produce a fiscal surplus thereafter. A lower uniform rate would also weaken the justification for exemptions, expanding the tax base and strengthening revenue productivity.  States ultimately receive 70.5 per cent of GST — 50 per cent directly as state GST and 20.5 per cent via the 41 per cent devolution of central GST. They also retain substantial taxing powers over alcohol, petroleum products, motor vehicles and property. Reforms of these taxes could offset transitional GST losses. Odisha, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra are working on revenue reforms, demonstrating the path to strengthen state finances without perpetuating GST distortions. 
 The writers are, respectively, a researcher at the XKDR Forum, and affiliated with the Pune International Centre and XKDR Forum.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Empty bank accounts in Vigilance Week expose gaps in banking oversight
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Empty bank accounts in Vigilance Week expose gaps in banking oversightEmpty bank accounts in Vigilance Week expose gaps in banking oversight

Are IT-trained staff available when regular operators are on leave? Are daily-waged support workers restricted to non-sensitive areas? Banks need to address these questions

premium

Representative image for bank

Tamal Bandyopadhyay8 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 8:11 PM ISTFarmer Vijendra Singh lost money kept with a bank. Singh told the media that his savings account at a branch of Punjab National Bank (PNB) in Greater Noida once held approximately ₹87–88 lakh, including compensation received from the authorities for land acquisition. When he checked, the balance had fallen to barely ₹1 lakh.  He is one of many depositors whose money, they allege, had disappeared from savings accounts and fixed deposits without their authorisation.  This happened in the last week of October when the banking industry was observing Vigilance Awareness Week.  Since 2000, every year, during the week that includes the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (October 31), a nationwide campaign has been organised by the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) to promote integrity, transparency, and the fight against corruption in public governance. This year, it was observed from October 26 to November 1 on the theme ‘Probity for Prosperity’.  Government departments, central public sector enterprises, public sector banks, and other participating organisations were directed to begin the observance with an integrity pledge. Workshops, outreach programmes, debates, quizzes,  and other awareness activities were also encouraged.  The vigilance-related activities are not confined to just one week. The CVC’s three-month preventive-vigilance campaign this year, running from August 17 to November 16, identifies five priorities: Disposal of pending complaints, disposal of pending cases, capacity building, digital initiatives, and transparency in contract management and awarding contracts to vendors. Work under these priority heads will continue till November 30.  The initiative is great. But, beyond meetings and posters, awareness must reach branch counters. All banks must remain vigilant 24/7 through an ever-aware oversight machinery. Not pledges and activities — the real scorecard is the number of vulnerable pockets closed within the system.  The Greater Noida allegations concern savings and fixed-deposit accounts, including those of farmers who had deposited land-compensation money. Customers say transactions occurred without their consent and allege that they received no SMS alerts. The bank concerned, I understand, has assured all aggrieved depositors of refunds within a few days. Media reports also hint at unauthorised access to lockers and growing anxiety among NRI customers. I have not been able to independently corroborate such allegations.  Scenes of distressed depositors waiting for explanations may evoke memories of troubled cooperative banks. But this bank is not insolvent, and only a tiny fraction of deposits is affected. Therefore, customers need not panic.  However, the institution’s immediate task is twofold: Establish the facts and prevent uncertainty from becoming a second injury. The bank’s preliminary inquiry identified approximately ₹ 10.24 crore in suspected unauthorised withdrawals, even as reconciliation continues to establish the full extent of the fraud. Earlier, customer allegations put the amount at nearly ₹ 35 crore, a figure that has not been officially confirmed.  A November 1 media report noted that a first information report (FIR) filed with the police mentions transactions worth ₹12.12 crore, while a branch staff member speaking anonymously told a social media channel that approximately 35 account holders had approached the police, with alleged unauthorised transactions pegged at around ₹17 crore.  These are overlapping investigative and complaint-based figures. By November 3, the Central Bureau of Investigation had reportedly arrested two individuals—a bank office assistant and an outsider—in connection with the alleged ₹ 10.24-crore fraud case. Arrest or suspension does not establish guilt, and the investigation into other possible accomplices and the movement of funds continues.  PNB’s October 30 statement said it had settled three claims totalling ₹43 lakh and would honour all genuine and valid claims. Going by the FIR, one woman depositor found three unfamiliar transactions dated September 16, 2026, when she updated her passbook. She had neither authorised nor consented to them.  The subsequent inquiry reportedly found that credentials belonging to six bank officials had been used for unauthorised transactions. Whether those credentials were shared voluntarily or compromised remains part of the investigation.  Other reported allegations include the manipulation of customer details and fixed-deposit records, premature closures, and diversion of funds through beneficiary accounts. The suspected activities had reportedly been going on for about three years. Why did the institution need a customer’s complaint to identify a pattern that its own internal controls should have flagged? The investigation must establish whether system alerts were absent, inadequately designed, ignored, or improperly closed. It must also determine which officials had access to the relevant information and what action they took.  National figures underline the gravity of the issue. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) Annual Report for 2025–26 records 10,114 fraud cases involving ₹48,021 crore, compared with 23,722 cases involving ₹32,803 crore in the preceding year. The data covers frauds of ₹1 lakh and above, and cases reported in a given year may relate to events from earlier years. Also, the FY2025-26 figure includes ₹30,199 crore relating to 314 older cases reported afresh following a re-examination. Crucially, the amount involved in reported frauds does not necessarily represent the final loss.  Reports of surprise inspections at PNB spoke of outsiders working inside banking areas, including cash counters and on branch computers. Initial reporting put the number of suspended branch heads at around 20. A recent media report revised the figure to around 50. Claims that suspensions may have reached nearly 100 remain unverified.  The bank’s inspection at the branches involved found that individuals — including insurance-company personnel, recovery agents, and other helpers — were allegedly assisting with core banking work amid claims of staffing shortages. Business correspondents, insurance representatives, and temporary workers may have legitimate, defined duties. But their presence does not justify access to another employee’s password, unrestricted customer information, or transaction-authorisation powers. Staffing shortages cannot be an excuse for password sharing, and management cannot treat staffing levels as unrelated to financial controls.  Can a branch maintain a genuine dual-control separation between the person entering a transaction and the person approving it? Are sufficiently IT-trained staff available when the regular operator of a specific desk goes on leave? Are support workers hired on a daily-wage basis properly engaged, supervised, and strictly restricted to non-sensitive areas? What happens when a manager formally reports that safe working arrangements cannot be maintained?  The reported reliance on informal helpers should prompt a serious re-examination of recruitment and deployment policies, including support-staff arrangements — rather than an assumption that daily-wage labour is an acceptable substitute for controlled system access.  Management must also examine whether third-party sales targets and other performance pressures leave sufficient time for the daily verification of transactions, reconciliation of all non-customer accounts, and prompt complaint handling.  Finally, auditors should examine repeated debits and credits, ledger reversals, connected beneficiaries, and changes to deposit instructions. They must scrutinise premature fixed deposit closures, changes to maturity-proceeds credit accounts, modifications to account operating details, registered mobile number alterations, disabled alert preferences, and unusual staff access patterns.  Following the RBI’s Master Direction on Fraud Risk Management (issued on July 31, 2026), banks require board-approved arrangements covering prevention, detection, investigation, staff accountability, recovery, and reporting. A dedicated board committee carries the responsibility for reviewing frauds, root causes, and corrective measures. The directions also call for early warning mechanisms covering non-credit banking transactions, with monitoring designed to promptly identify unusual activity. PNB’s experience with the 2018 Nirav Modi scandal makes the need for durable institutional learning particularly vital. Following that event, the RBI discontinued Letters of Undertaking (LoUs) for import trade credit.  For a depositor awaiting access to savings, a mere institutional explanation is not a resolution. The bank should provide a dedicated claims officer, written acknowledgements, clear verification requirements, and regular progress updates. Restoration of funds must transparently cover applicable interest alongside the principal amount, without unjust charges. For Singh and other complainants, the test is not whether employees raised their hands to take a pledge during Vigilance Awareness Week. It is whether the institution can explain what happened, restore legitimate claims, and demonstrate that the next depositor will not face the same ordeal.  Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel’s standard for public service remains a fitting measure of that responsibility. In 1947, while addressing civil service probationers, Patel said: “No service worth the name can claim to exist if it does not have in view the achievement of the highest standard of integrity.”

entry.title: What to prioritise: Debt repayment, insurance, or investing your money?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / What to prioritise: Debt repayment, insurance, or investing your money?What to prioritise: Debt repayment, insurance, or investing your money?

An investment plan should begin with financial protection and debt repayment, not market returns

premium

Financial planning for young professionals should begin with adequate insurance and debt repayment before moving to investments, says Harsh Roongta. | Representative Picture

Harsh Roongta4 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 8:09 PM ISTI was talking to Rohini, who had just got her commercial pilot licence and begun her first job with an airline. She wanted my advice on investing the monthly surplus from her salary. She had an education loan at 8 per cent interest, with eight years to run. Her surplus was what remained after the hefty equated monthly instalment (EMI). I told her there was an order to follow. First, pay the fixed EMI on the loan. Second, buy the right insurance. Third, use the balance to repay the loan faster. Investing comes after that.She was shocked. “I thought an investment adviser would tell me where to invest. Instead, you ask me to buy insurance, though you write against it in your columns. And you want me to repay my loan faster.”  After her shock wore off, I explained my position. I have always written against the mis-selling of insurance. Yet the right insurance comes before any investment. Rohini said she had no dependants, so she did not need term insurance. But she herself depended on her income. That income needed protection. She needed two covers: a critical illness policy that pays a lump sum on diagnosis of a listed illness and an accidental disability policy that pays if an accident disables her permanently. That money would replace her lost income.The airline already gave sufficient cover for both risks. It also covered her medical costs. I told her to buy her own medical policy. It is unwise to depend solely on an employer’s policy.  That brought us to step three: repaying the loan faster. Rohini had two fears. The first was liquidity. Investments could be redeemed in an emergency, but could she access money used to prepay the loan? Her lender allowed her to withdraw any amount she had prepaid. She could also build an emergency fund from the surplus before beginning loan prepayment. The fear of missing out (FOMO) came second. Her friends were making returns from all kinds of ideas. She would be stuck with the boring task of repaying a loan.  My response was simple. I asked her if she would borrow at 8 per cent to invest in any idea, however good. She was horrified at the thought. I told her investing her surplus instead of repaying the loan was the same thing. It is borrowing to invest. Repaying the loan early saves her interest at a rate of 8 per cent. Equity could earn more over 8-10 years, but that return is uncertain. Returns can come in bursts after long spells of losses. She may lose patience and quit at the wrong time. A systematic investment plan (SIP) can be stopped. An EMI cannot. In uncertain times, it is best to have as little committed repayment as possible.  Rohini said her father might clear the loan. Where would she then invest her surplus? Her friends were investing in cryptocurrencies, unlisted shares, unregulated start-ups and initial public offerings (IPOs). I told her to avoid such get-rich-quick ideas. She should save 30 per cent of her salary every month. Her living costs and insurance premiums must fit within the rest. She should not wait for the perfect investment. At this stage of her career, the compounding of her savings habit matters more than the compounding of her investments. I suggested a simple passive fund: an index, multi-asset or hybrid fund. If choosing was hard, even a bank recurring deposit would do.  Truth be told, Rohini expected an investment adviser to tell her where to invest. But an adviser must look at her financial life, beginning with whether she should invest at all. My advice was boring and gave her no bragging rights. She understood the reasoning and followed it. She bought the right insurance. She cleared the loan from her own income, though her father could have helped, and then started a monthly SIP in a passive multi-asset fund. Good advice is like a kandeel on a dark path. It does not dazzle. It lights the next few steps. I wish every reader the same light and the courage to follow it.

entry.title: No room for pessimism as India's economy continues to show resilience
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / No room for pessimism as India's economy continues to show resilienceNo room for pessimism as India's economy continues to show resilience

India's strong economic fundamentals and normalising valuations could create an opportunity for equities to recover after two years of underperformance

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Prashant Jain6 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 8:08 PM IST“In the short run, the market is a voting machine, but in the long run, it is a weighing machine.” - Benjamin Graham This quote reminds us that while near-term market returns are volatile and uncertain, long-term market performance is linked to the growth of underlying businesses. Given this background, it is surprising to see that the weak market returns of the past two years are driving pessimism around India, especially when its economy has shown remarkable resilience even in an adverse environment. We must remember that equities are slaves to corporate earnings in the long term, not the other way around.  India’s economy continues to deliver strong growth. This economic strength is built on strong macro parameters. The current account deficit is low, the fiscal deficit is well-controlled, bank balance sheets are healthy, and corporate leverage is at historic lows. Meanwhile, corporate profit growth remains strong, and aggregate capital expenditure is growing faster than gross domestic product (GDP).   The Indian economy has grown  at approximately 7.5 per cent annually across FY25 and FY26 in an adverse environment: Net foreign direct investment (FDI) was nearly zero, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) sold heavily, gold imports remained elevated, and oil prices were volatile. What is even more impressive is that during the first quarter of FY27, when crude averaged roughly $97 per barrel, the economy still delivered an impressive 7.8 per cent growth.   The sustained growth during this difficult period was aided by proactive management from the government and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Interventions such as lower goods and services tax rates, reduced excise duties on petrol and diesel, and the absorption of higher fertiliser and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) costs helped sustain strong domestic demand. Furthermore, the timely mobilisation of $136 billion through Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) or FCNR(B) and external commercial borrowings has sharply improved India’s forex reserves and balance of payments (BOP). This has improved sentiment toward the rupee, which in turn is supportive of capital flows. Healthy reserves improve the resilience of India in the medium term to higher oil prices and higher US yields. Additionally, India has significantly reduced its structural vulnerability to energy shocks, with oil imports as a share of GDP declining from over 5 per cent in FY2013 to around 3 per cent in FY2026.  Looking ahead, the outlook for the Indian economy is even better. India is widely known as the services leader of the world – with its share of global services (excluding tourism) around 8 per cent – and is proving resilient to artificial intelligence (AI) disruption so far. Despite negative sentiment regarding the impact of AI on information technology exports, India's services exports grew 15 per cent year-to-date (till August). What’s more, India is making good progress in manufacturing. This structural shift is driven by multiple catalysts: China’s per-capita income is now 5x that of India, making Indian labour competitive; supportive government policies; rupee depreciation vs Chinese Yuan (CNY); a focus on the ‘China+1’ strategy by developed nations seeking to diversify their supply chains; and supportive capital markets. Consequently, the manufacturing sector is now growing faster than overall GDP and, given its low base, this growth should be sustained for many years.   The external environment is also gradually becoming supportive. Net FDI has started to climb, and gold prices are losing momentum, which should reduce the demand for imports. FPI selling will abate at some point and oil prices will eventually come down once the West Asia conflict calms, as the oil market is fundamentally oversupplied over the medium term, given the impending global transition toward electric vehicles.   So, if the economy and its outlook is so robust, why did the markets underperform over the past two years? The underperformance was due to elevated starting valuations, the AI trade, and primary market supply.  This period marked the emergence of an AI and semiconductor supercycle. Because India lacks direct exposure to these sectors, it effectively became a funding source for FPIs, driving significant capital outflows and causing Indian equities to sharply underperform the broader emerging markets index. It is not that India’s economy was faltering; rather, markets with heavy exposure to hardware stocks — where earnings were temporarily growing exponentially — simply offered more immediate, momentum-driven returns. This has driven India’s five-year performance relative to emerging markets to a record low and should mean revert at some point.  In addition to the $60 billion in FPI outflows over the past two years, a constant supply of new equity has absorbed domestic mutual fund inflows, limiting the upward movement of secondary stock prices. However, this availability of capital via initial public offerings (IPOs) is beneficial for the real economy. It allows companies across the manufacturing, services, and consumer sectors to fund expansions, which in turn drives employment and consumption.   After two years of time-consolidation and a modest price correction, valuation multiples have now normalised. Global headwinds for India also appear to be easing as US 10-year yields retreat below 5 per cent and the momentum behind the AI trade cools, with the Korean market (MSCI South Korea) down around 35 per cent from its recent peak. Encouragingly, on October 30, when the US Semiconductor Index (SOX) was down 7.2 per cent and the Nasdaq dropped 2 per cent, Indian ADRs (American depository receipts) held firm. If the AI theme wanes, the Indian market will stand in a much better light.  To summarise, India’s relevance to the global economy is growing steadily, and as the world’s fastest-growing major economy, its global footprint will only expand in the years to come. Over the past 25 years, India’s share of world GDP has increased from 1.4 per cent to 3.3 per cent. Today, it is the sixth-largest economy in the world and is anticipated to become the third-largest in three to four years, crossing $5 trillion in nominal GDP.  In contrast to the strong and sustained economic growth, equity returns are non-linear and bunched up. Hence, Indian equities have played catch-up after every prolonged period of underperformance. Over the past 25 years, following every two-year drawdown of 15 per cent or more, the subsequent three-year returns have been significant, and we do not see any reason why it should be different this time. Rather than a cause for pessimism, this divergence creates a compelling opportunity for discerning investors. 
The writer is Chief Investment Officer of 3P Investment Managers, a SEBI-registered AIF. entry.title: Exim matters: US verdict lifts hopes; mkts celebrate, but traders cautious
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Exim matters: US verdict lifts hopes; mkts celebrate, but traders cautiousExim matters: US verdict lifts hopes; mkts celebrate, but traders cautious

Democratic control of Congress could increase scrutiny of Trump's policies, but Indian businesses must prepare for continued tariff uncertainty, geopolitical risks and shifting trade dynamics

premium

The Democratic victory in the US midterm elections has raised hopes of easing trade and geopolitical tensions, but uncertainty over President Donald Trump's policies persists. | Image: Bloomberg

TNC Rajagopalan Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 8:05 PM ISTLast week, Indian equity markets brought cheer ahead of Diwali, with the Sensex gaining 8.8 per cent and the Nifty 50 advancing 8.6 per cent despite a global technology sell-off. The Democratic Party’s victory in the US midterm elections raised hopes of easing geopolitical and trade tensions. For exporters and importers, the test is whether political change will bring commercial relief.  Democrats will control both houses of the US Congress from January, but Donald Trump remains President until January 20, 2029. Congress can investigate his administration, scrutinise expenditure and challenge his policies. However, he retains substantial authority over diplomacy, military operations and tariffs. Expectations of an immediate change in American policy should therefore remain modest.  Pressure to end the Iran war should increase because its economic costs have become a political liability for Republicans. Freer flows of Gulf oil and gas could ease energy prices, lower production and transport costs worldwide, and support demand in importing economies. Indian businesses would benefit through more dependable supplies, lower costs and potentially stronger export orders.  However, ending hostilities would not necessarily restore shipping on pre-war terms. Iran seeks revenue connected with passage through Hormuz, while an Omani proposal envisages voluntary contributions under regional management. Any compulsory charge could leave a continuing burden, although reliable passage and lower insurance premiums could reduce total costs. Restoring normal shipping through the Red Sea would require separate progress involving Yemen’s Houthis. A durable settlement in Ukraine could similarly improve Black Sea shipping and ease uncertainty over grain and fertiliser supplies. Democratic control of Congress, however, does not by itself bring a settlement closer.  On tariffs, congressional hearings and political pressure could encourage exemptions and negotiated reductions. Nevertheless, a Democratic majority cannot by itself reverse duties imposed under powers already delegated to the President. Legislation curtailing those powers could face his veto, requiring two-thirds support in each chamber to overcome it. Nor does opposition to Trump imply support for unrestricted trade. Protecting American manufacturing and strategic industries remains politically attractive. Greater consultation with allies could ease disputes, but a cooperative approach cannot be assumed. Continued barriers could divert goods towards other markets, intensifying competition and encouraging further protectionism.  For Indian traders, lower costs would be welcome, but improved competitiveness in the American market would depend on the tariff treatment of rival suppliers. A reduction in duties on Indian goods would offer little competitive advantage if competing countries secured even larger concessions. Goods redirected from the US could also intensify competition, putting pressure on domestic manufacturers’ margins.  India should, therefore, pursue a commercially worthwhile bilateral trade agreement without sacrificing substance for an early signature. Ministers have reported negotiating progress. The test is whether the terms deliver durable market access, favourable tariffs relative to competitors and protection against subsequent measures eroding the concessions. Businesses need arrangements on which they can base prices, orders and investment.  The election has altered Washington’s political balance, but Trump’s unpredictability could still unsettle markets, disrupt contracts and delay investment. Indian traders should, therefore, prepare for abrupt policy shifts while diversifying markets and strengthening their own competitiveness.  Markets have welcomed the prospect of better days. Traders will look for those hopes to find expression in lower costs, dependable supplies and durable agreements. May this Diwali herald lasting peace and shared prosperity. My best wishes to readers and their families.

entry.title: Delhi's pollution crisis needs cleaner public transport, not shutdowns
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Delhi's pollution crisis needs cleaner public transport, not shutdownsDelhi's pollution crisis needs cleaner public transport, not shutdowns

Delhi's winter pollution plan relies on restrictions, while gaps in public transport and cleaner alternatives remain unaddressed, argues Sunita Narain.

premium

Delhi’s winter pollution crisis highlights the need for sustained action on vehicular and industrial emissions, better public transport and cleaner fuel alternatives, rather than relying primarily on temporary restrictions, argues Sunita Narain. (Representative Image)

Sunita Narain5 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 7:53 PM ISTDelhi’s season of despair has started with winter setting in. When you read this, it is likely the city will have slipped into the category of “very severe” pollution. It is a time when toxins settle closer to the ground and choke us. This will be worse on windless days and on days when winds bring smoke from neighbouring fields where stubble is being burned. The question every year is: What have we done to make this season less harmful?  The good news is that the Delhi government has announced steps to tackle winter pollution. The bad news is that these measures are, at best, half-hearted and weak, and, worse, they signal completely giving up on pollution control. The action plan is about shutting down the city, putting the onus on the public to suspend day-to-day activities. I say this knowing fully well that activities like driving to work add to pollution.  The sheer number of private cars and two-wheelers is a major contributor to air pollution. But the plan works only when commuters have viable alternatives, such as adequate and augmented public transport and roads where people can cycle or walk, before directing us to work at 50 per cent capacity for the coming three months — from November to January.  The government has taken a page from the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) playbook, without a clue of what this really means. Let me explain, as I was among those involved in taking the idea of GRAP to the Supreme Court. This was in 2016, when I was a member of the erstwhile Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA) for the National Capital Region (NCR), and reporting to the court.  We proposed GRAP as a smog-alert emergency measure — not as a substitute for real action. It was called “graded” because restrictions would be introduced based on the severity of air pollution. The EPCA also took to the court the matter of trucks and other heavy-duty vehicles passing through Delhi. This added enormously to pollution. The court levied a congestion or pollution tax on the entry of these vehicles and pressed the Union government to expedite the construction of alternative bypass expressways. Over the next two years, many decisive and tough actions were directed, including the fast transition to Bharat Stage VI fuel and vehicle technology.  When the court gave the green signal to GRAP in 2016, it was cognisant of the disruption it would cause. Closing schools, for instance, would come at the cost of education and create problems for parents. It was not a measure that could be taken lightly.  In the original GRAP, notified by the Union government in 2017, schools were to close only on days when the air quality index deteriorated to the “severe” or “public emergency” category. Governments could introduce restrictions on heavy-duty vehicles entering the city and on plying private vehicles. The objective was to limit these measures to days when necessary and, meanwhile, to keep taking steps so that the measures would not be necessary. The inconvenience would prod governments to take year-long hard action. Shutdowns were not policy.  The government may argue that this is its grand plan. But frankly, there is no merit in this. Pollution-control measures are either half-baked, inadequate, or without the full-throated determination needed to clean up the air of Delhi-NCR.  Why do I say this? Two issues will clear the air. The first is the number of vehicles plying on Delhi’s roads. The only real way ahead is a time-bound plan to augment public transport, not just in Delhi but across the NCR and between its cities. We also need to make the transition to cleaner vehicles — electric buses, taxis, and three-wheelers should complement the electrified metro. Based on the EPCA’s recommendations, the court had laid the foundations for this by 2019 — it directed (in 1998 and reiterated again and again) the need for at least 10,000 buses in the city, large or small.  It cleared the way for the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation to expand its network and for the first high-speed rail corridor (Delhi-Meerut) to be built.  Obviously, much more needs to be done, particularly to interconnect the NCR so that it moves as one and to connect different modes of transport so that we can travel, switch, and reach our destination in affordable and convenient ways. But what we are doing is too little, too late.  Today, Delhi has only about 6,840 buses, instead of 10,000. Other cities of the NCR virtually have nothing for interconnections. The Delhi government’s plan to electrify its bus fleet is notable, but with this we need a plan to increase ridership and provide a viable alternative to people as they shift from personal cars.  The second, and finally, is the issue of industrial pollution from factories operating in unauthorised areas in and around the city. These have been directed to stop using coal, but there is little effort to ensure that viable alternatives are available, whether reliable and cheaper electricity or natural gas. I could go on. But my gripe is that we are not acting at scale, by taking tough and time-bound action to bend the pollution curve.

entry.title: AI brings alive India's ancient knowledge through modern technology
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / AI brings alive India's ancient knowledge through modern technologyAI brings alive India's ancient knowledge through modern technology

AI, digital storytelling and manuscript digitisation are helping revive Indian mythology and ancient scientific knowledge, making cultural heritage more accessible to younger generations.

premium

AI and digital technologies are giving Indian mythology and ancient knowledge new reach, helping creators reinterpret epics for younger audiences while enabling researchers to study and preserve centuries-old manuscripts.

Pranjal Sharma3 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 5:54 PM ISTIn the festival season, technology is helping bring alive ancient stories, epic dramas and mythologies for a new generation of Indians.  Social media creators are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) and digital content tools to reimagine Indian mythology for younger audiences. AI-art storytellers use generative AI platforms such as Midjourney, DALL-E and Runway to create cinematic depictions of scenes from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, transforming ancient stories into visually rich reels and short videos. Mythology-focused influencers are also using motion graphics and visual effects to recreate legendary events such as the Kurukshetra war, Hanuman’s journey to Sri Lanka and Krishna’s teachings in ways that feel relatable and modern.  AI voiceovers, animated illustrations and digital avatars are being used to narrate lesser-known stories from the Puranas and regional folklore, making them more accessible to younger audiences. Other creators employ augmented reality filters that allow users to interact with mythological themes, characters and symbols through Instagram Stories and Reels. Animated creators, including those behind digital channels inspired by Amar Chitra Katha-style storytelling, are adapting traditional narratives into short, shareable video formats that blend historical interpretation with contemporary visual language.  The result is that ancient epics and mythologies are reaching millions of young Indians through immersive, technology-enabled storytelling. By combining AI-generated imagery, animation, special effects, audio technology and social media algorithms, influencers are helping keep cultural narratives relevant and engaging in the digital age.  Technology is also being used to examine and validate aspects of ancient Indian science by analysing historical texts, archaeological evidence, linguistic patterns and astronomical references. Researchers are applying machine learning and natural language processing to Sanskrit manuscripts, including the Vedas, Aryabhata’s astronomical works and Sushruta’s medical texts, to better understand historical dating and early empirical knowledge. AI tools are also helping scholars map astronomical observations described in ancient epics and compare them with modern celestial models.  Researchers at institutions including the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) have applied natural language processing to ancient mathematical, astronomical and medical manuscripts. This is making large collections of texts searchable and helping scholars identify scientific concepts systematically. The effort has revealed sophisticated treatments of grammar, mathematics and astronomy in works such as Aryabhata’s Aryabhatiya and Bhaskaracharya’s Lilavati.  A recent example is the use of AI and machine learning in Ayurgenomics, which combines principles from Ayurveda with modern genetics. The initiative has been highlighted by both the World Health Organization and India's Ministry of AYUSH as an example of AI being used to investigate whether traditional Ayurvedic classifications correlate with measurable biological and genetic traits.  This year, the Ministry of Culture's Gyan Bharatam initiative began piloting AI systems that can read, transcribe, search and analyse Sanskrit manuscripts on mathematics, astronomy, medicine and other traditional disciplines. These tools are helping researchers uncover, compare and validate scientific concepts buried in manuscript collections. IIT Bombay-based BharatGen is working with the ministry on an active pilot, building AI tools that help people read these texts, learn from them and recite them correctly.  Museums, libraries and archives are digitising manuscripts, paintings, photographs and ancient texts to prevent deterioration and make them widely accessible. Institutions such as the National Digital Library of India and the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts have created digital repositories containing millions of cultural artefacts. High-resolution scanning allows fragile documents, including palm-leaf manuscripts and rare books, to be preserved without repeated physical handling.  As AI advances, it is helping India understand its own heritage better.

entry.title: Bharat Ratna LK Advani Ji at 100!
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Bharat Ratna LK Advani Ji at 100!Bharat Ratna LK Advani Ji at 100!

A former Deputy Prime Minister and one of India's longest-serving Home Ministers, Lal Krishna Advani Ji is one of the few people whose lives have touched many different chapters of modern India

premium

Senior BJP leader LK Advani turns 99 today, marking the beginning of his 100th year.

Narendra Modi New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 6:00 AM ISTShri Lal Krishna Advani Ji enters the hundredth year of his life today, November 8. This year, his birthday fittingly coincides with Diwali, a festival associated with Prabhu Shri Ram and the diya at a time when we are marking 75 years since the inception of the Jana Sangh, the 125th Jayanti of Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee, and recently celebrated a hundred years of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).   There are very few people whose lives have touched so many different chapters of modern India. Advani Ji was born on November 8, 1927, on Dev Deepawali. As a youngster in 1947, he experienced the pain of leaving behind his familiar world in Sindh. He rebuilt his life from scratch without bitterness. This trait of being able to build from scratch, against all odds, has stayed with him throughout. It was seen while he was strengthening the Jana Sangh and later building the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). His tenures as BJP President saw the Congress falling sharply from 400 to below 200 in 1989 and the BJP becoming the single-largest party for the first time in 1996. Advani Ji nurtured generations of karyakartas and gave the party a clear foundation rooted in the principle of ‘Nation First’.   Two qualities always set Advani Ji apart as a leader. First, his ideological clarity and intellectual sharpness. This was reflected in his speeches and writings. The Jana Sangh and BJP resolutions he authored remain worth reading even today, while his interviews were consistently incisive and precise. Second, the manner in which he exposed the pseudo-secularism propounded by a large section of the Indian polity for many years.    Advani Ji took up every responsibility with immense diligence. As an RSS pracharak, Advani Ji first worked in different parts of Rajasthan. From there, he went to the national capital, where he started working closely with Atal Ji. History shows that it is rare for two towering political leaders to work together for several decades, cooperating with each other without becoming competitors. Advani Ji and Atal Ji set a remarkable example. Together, they changed the course of Indian politics.  The Delhi that Advani Ji came to was coming to terms with the horrors of Partition. He immersed himself in making the Jana Sangh stronger. In 1967, Advani Ji became the Chairman of the Delhi Metropolitan Council, where he worked alongside the late Vijay Kumar Malhotra Ji (who became Chief Executive Councillor).   In 1970, Advani Ji’s Parliamentary innings began. His interventions have won appreciation across the political spectrum. He made a mark as an Member of Parliament (MP) and later, as Leader of Opposition in both houses and from the treasury benches, too. Despite Parliamentary commitments, he frequently travelled across India meeting people.    I vividly recall the 1991 Lok Sabha elections. It was decided that Advani Ji would contest the Lok Sabha elections from two seats, one of which was Gandhinagar. He had an old link with Gujarat. His father had settled in Kutch after Partition. Advani Ji had also served as a Rajya Sabha MP from Gujarat. So, it was a homecoming of sorts. Being involved in the BJP organisation, I had the honour of helping prepare his papers and assisting him throughout the campaign. The people of Gandhinagar sent him to Parliament time and again. As a voter of Gandhinagar, I also had the honour of voting for Advani Ji on numerous occasions. The care and attention he devoted to his constituency is something to learn from.   The Emergency was a watershed moment in Advani Ji’s life. He was at the forefront of saving democracy and protecting the Constitution. His experiences found their way into his book, ‘A Prisoner's Scrap-Book.’ One part of that book, titled ‘A Tale of Two Emergencies’, beautifully explained the striking similarities between the events in India starting June 1975 and those in Nazi Germany in 1933.   Advani Ji was a fiery Opposition leader but an equally excellent administrator. When the Janata Government came to office in 1977, Advani Ji became Minister for Information and Broadcasting. It is widely accepted that his work in this department was extremely impactful. As Deputy Prime Minister and one of India’s longest-serving Home Ministers, he was instrumental in strengthening India’s security apparatus. His work in improving the lives of our security forces is remembered with great fondness. His unequivocal stand against terrorism ensured India got a tough anti-terror law.   Of course, an iconic moment in Advani Ji’s life was the Somnath to Ayodhya Rath Yatra. It changed the course of Indian society for the better. I consider it a privilege that I got the opportunity to be involved in this yatra from the ideation stage to execution. Being present at Somnath when the yatra began was particularly special. A yatra can be very demanding, requiring long hours, constant travel, physical endurance and an ability to remain focused despite fatigue. Advani Ji embodied this endurance.  I also have memories of the saddening moments of Advani Ji’s arrest in Bihar. Then, in Gujarat, the BJP withdrew support from the Chimanbhai Patel government. With this, a simple message was given, that when it comes to our ideology and the Ram Temple, there will never be any compromise. Many of our senior leaders and karyakartas took an oath that, come what may, a Ram Temple will be built. And, years later, with the blessings of the people of India, a grand Mandir for Prabhu Shri Ram became a reality in Ayodhya.   There is so much more of Advani Ji that is outstanding. His simplicity, for example. After the Navnirman Movement, Advani Ji had come to Junagadh and stayed for a month as an ordinary karyakarta, preparing the party for the Assembly elections in which the Congress was rejected. He has always shown what probity in public life is about. He is a voracious reader. Those who have spent time with him know how carefully he goes through newspapers. He is a big fan of cinema and theatre, and has been an enthusiastic film critic. His sense of history and the need to preserve it is visible in his book, ‘My Country My Life’.  Advani Ji always remained in touch with Sindhi culture. Another effort he undertook was the popularisation of Sindhu Darshan Puja near Leh. I myself have been to one puja with Advani Ji and George Fernandes Ji.   Any account of Advani Ji’s remarkable journey would be incomplete without mentioning Kamla Advani Ji. She was a constant source of strength and support throughout his public life.  Growing up in Karachi, Advani Ji could hardly have imagined the path his life would take. In an expression of gratitude, the people of India conferred upon him the Bharat Ratna in 2024. As Advani Ji enters the hundredth year of his life, I pray that he be blessed with good health and that he continues to inspire us all as he has always done.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Narendra Modi LK Advani Bharat Ratna

entry.title: A 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' test: Risks of reforms without consultation
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / A 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' test: Risks of reforms without consultationA 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' test: Risks of reforms without consultation

Between the farm laws and Agnipath, you could say the Modi government erred in taking its most loyal constituencies for granted: Hindi-heartland farmers and soldiers

Representative Picture

Shekhar Gupta7 min read Last Updated : Nov 07 2026 | 11:53 AM ISTYou can find a more diplomatic or politically convenient description for it, but the Modi government’s latest move on the Agniveer scheme, brought in with such aplomb, is a rollback. More so, a poll-eve capitulation. Seventy-five per cent of the first lot of Agniveers would have finished their tour of duty, or walked the Agnipath (path of fire), as the scheme was named, and returned to their hometowns and villages by December. It’s just that many would have gone back to Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Punjab, even Manipur, all going to the polls this coming February. All are traditionally major catchment areas for armed forces recruitment. For the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the first two are much too vital to risk.  The prospect of these demobilised soldiers returning and joining opposition rallies, even enrolling in something like the Cockroach Janta Party, was scary for the BJP which, until the other day, was riding an all-conquering confidence. Now, it was seen as a risk not worth taking. On top of these, in November or thereabouts next year, Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat will have their state elections. Gujarat, the BJP can still be calm about. But Himachal, a stronghold it lost to the Congress last time, is a traditional recruiting area with a large ex-servicemen’s constituency.

Also Read

 The party has now become far too risk-averse to put to the electoral test what was once its favourite reform. Reform it was, though. And we’ll talk about how, and then why it collapsed at its first test. There are three things governments are remembered for. Then there’s a fourth category: The good ideas a government implements and then withdraws under pressure or in panic. The good and the bad ideas are the first two. The third is the good ideas they propose but lack the nerve or skills to implement. We can list many of the United Progressive Alliance’s (UPA’s), for example: Aadhaar and India Stack based on it, direct benefit transfer (DBT) of welfare, even targeted delivery of subsidised cooking gas only to the poor and deserving. So were its many grand and audacious infrastructure projects of national importance. All got caught either in its indecision loop, internal party-versus-government contradictions, or ideological opposition. Most were subsequently consummated by the Modi government. Think the rail link to Srinagar, Mumbai Metro, Trans Harbour Link, the new Expressways, completion of the dedicated freight corridors (DFCs) and even the annihilation of armed Maoism. All of these were UPA projects abandoned midway. The Modi government did a brilliant job with these. It just tripped up on some of its own ideas. In journalism, we follow the three-example rule, meaning that these make a straight line. Or your argument. For Modi government’s rollbacks, count the farm laws, brought in with such self-assurance in 2020 and rolled back in their entirety in 2021 in the face of opposition from farmers. The second is now the Agniveer scheme. For the third, my preference would be the caste Census. The Modi government was opposed to it forever, then suddenly included it in the delayed 2021 Census being carried out now. This was under Rahul Gandhi’s pressure. If you don’t think that’s strong enough to make the third example —although I think it does, given the implications — I can give you another. The Prime Minister repeatedly derided the freebie culture, or what he contemptuously dismissed as “revdi” culture. Speaking at the inauguration of the Bundelkhand Expressway at Jalaun in UP in July 2022, he said, “This revdi culture is very dangerous for the development of the country. Those with revdi culture will never build new expressways, new airports or defence corridors for you.” And then, around the time of the Chhattisgarh elections in the winter of 2023, he announced that the Covid-era free food grain scheme would continue. In the same set of elections, the BJP brought in the Ladli Behna Yojana for cash transfers to women. Then, probably stung by the loss of majority in 2024, the party unleashed an almighty revdi “revolution”, with payouts reaching up to  ₹10,000 as a one-time transfer in Bihar and a promise of  ₹2 lakh if the woman started an enterprise. This was so expensive that even a rich state like Maharashtra is struggling to pay out, looking for excuses to reduce the number of beneficiaries. Women are already protesting, saying they’ve been denied their “Ladki Bahin” payouts. If you prefer, you can list this as the third example. However you look at it, this government has lost much of its appetite for risk, even with reforms where it had shown great conviction and commitment. These four examples are enough to show that the Modi government will also be remembered for the really good ideas it brought in, Agnipath included, and rolled back. This column, for the record, had supported each of these ideas. Between the farm laws and Agnipath, you could say the Modi government failed the test of both elements of the “ Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan” sentiment. It erred in taking its most significant and loyal constituencies for granted: Hindi heartland farmers and soldiers. The most disappointing thing is how it failed to reach out to them and build acceptance for such radical changes. People are by and large suspicious of major policy shifts with such significant implications for their lives, particularly when introduced through a shock-and-awe approach. That, however, has been this government’s style. Think sudden demonetisation or the Covid lockdown. Decisions affecting farmers and soldiers were taken in much the same way. Unlike the first two, which came with an end date, these policy changes were meant to survive in perpetuity. That explains the pushback from the base, and the Modi government’s rollback. Governance remains a painstaking, laborious, even boring business because it requires background work, scenario-mapping, war-gaming, or what the armed forces would call staff work. That is what the civil services and bureaucracies are there for. The absence of this precise element has bedevilled these plans — surprising, given how heavily the Modi government depends on civil servants. Were they asked to do their homework, or handed the decision first? There may be a concern that decisions could get caught in an analysis-paralysis loop. But you can’t always be like a commando who jumps out of a plane without checking the parachute. That isn’t fearless. It’s reckless. When Agnipath was implemented, it was well known that the first lot would leave on the eve of these state elections. An extensive rehabilitation programme, beginning midway through their four years, could have cushioned the blow. Now, the baby is gone, and with it the bathwater. The same lack of homework preceded the implementation of One Rank, One Pension (OROP). It was an election promise, all parties agreed with it, and no Indian would begrudge soldiers this benefit. But if the additional costs had been calculated and a necessary top-up provided to the defence budget, the story might have been different. The sudden increase in pensions because of OROP came from a defence budget that didn’t even keep pace with inflation over the years. This shrank the capital or acquisition budget. As concerns grew, Agnipath was rolled out in a hurry. Poor staff work created two kinds of soldiers, two sets of wages and even two sets of benefits for families in the event of a battle fatality. Most significant armies now have soldiers serving short tenures. But they don’t treat conscripted soldiers as a category separate from those on full-career service. Here, they were even addressed separately. Each unit then had an Agniveer sub-unit within it. This was unsustainable. The twin ideas of reducing the pension burden going ahead and making the armed forces much younger were both virtuous. Both have been lost to poor planning, hasty implementation and now withdrawal. This first batch will finish its sixth year on the eve of the 2029 general election. Rescuing this good idea will be a political miracle. It’s looking like a case of na khuda hi mila, na visaal-e-sanam (neither did I find God, nor my beloved).
